list.listitem: Suspect cutaneous (CL), mucocutaneous (MCL) or mucosal (ML) leishmaniasis in patients with a history of a painless, non-healing skin, nasal, or oral lesion after exposure in an endemic region. Diagnosis is made by sampling affected tissue for histopathology/culture/PCR. Species ID allows risk assessment of mucosal involvement to guide treatment. C

Suspect visceral leishmaniasis (VL) in patients with fever, pancytopenia, malaise, weight loss, and hepatosplenomegaly. Diagnosis is by bone marrow biopsy for microscopy/histopathology/culture/PCR/serology. C

Local CL can heal spontaneously with scarring. Complicated CL (with multiple lesions) requires oral or parenteral systemic therapy. Options include azoles, miltefosine, afphotericine B, and pertavalent antimonials. B
MCL, ML, and VL, require systemic therapy with amphotericin B (L-AmB), pentavalent antimonials, or miltefosine. B

Prevention strategies include clothing to cover exposed skin, bed nets, climate controlled sleeping areas, and insecticides. Community strategies include rapid ID and treatement of cases, sand fly vector control, animal vaccination, and culling of affected animals. B

Contact the CDC (404-718-4745) or the Leishmania Diagnostic Laboratory at the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research (240-595-7353) for assistance in diagnosis and management. See attached CDC guideline for specimen collection. C

background.definition: Leishmaniasis is a protozoal disease, transmitted by the bite of over 90 species of sand flies, causing cutaneous, mucosal, and visceral infection depending on the infecting species. Caused by more than 20 species of the protozoan parasite Leishmania, some species cause cutaneous (CL) and/or mucosal (ML) leishmaniasis, while other species are associated with visceral (systemic) leishmaniasis (VL), also known as Kala-Azar. Leishmaniasis is classified as a Neglected Tropical Disease (NTD).

list.listitem: Cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) is the most common form, with an estimated 700,000 to 1.2 million new cases annually.
CL cases are roughly divided by one-third each in South/Central America, the Mediterranean region, and Western Asia. Worldwide incidence by country based on WHO data is shown in
Visceral leishmaniasis (VL), or Kala-Azar, is less common with 50,000-90,000 new cases annually. Worldwide incidence by country is shown in .
More than 90% of VL cases are in India, Bangladesh, Sudan, South Sudan, Ethiopia, and Brazil, with sporadic cases elsewhere.

Leishmaniasis is a disease of poverty or immunocompromised state and one of the world's most neglected tropical diseases. It ranks second among tropical diseases in disability-adjusted life-years behind malaria.
Leishmaniasis epidemics are often found in areas of conflict and displacement.
The disfiguring sequelae of CL and ML often leads to social stigmatization, rejection by partners, and creates a high risk of developing psychological problems.

CL is caused by L.L. tropica and L.L. major in Asia, the Middle East, Africa, L. infantum in Southern Europe, and L. aethiopica in East Africa. In the Americas there are many species that cause cutaneous leishmaniasis. Several species belonging to the Viannia subgroup are the most common causes of ML.

VL is caused by L. donovani in Asia and East Africa and L. infantum/L. chagasi in the Mediterranean and Americas regions. L. donovani, and to a large extent L.tropica, has only anthroponotic (spread from humans to others with humans as a reservoir) transmission, but L. infantum like CL has many mammalian animal reservoirs (most importantly dogs, but also rodents and small mammals) and is considered a zoonosis. Most reservoir animals are not ill, but dogs and cats can get sick and die from leishmaniasis.
Leishmania is transmitted by the bite of phlebotomine sand flies.
VL can also be transmitted congenitally and by IVDU, transfusion, transplantation.
Leishmanial amastigotes (matured from phagocytized promastigotes) are intracellular protozoa of the family Trypanosomatidae. The infection is primarily of macrophages and is chronic and persistent.

The clinical manifestations of leishmaniasis depend on complex interactions between the parasite virulence factors and the cell-mediated immune system of the host. Leishmania evade the immune system by resisting complement attack, maniupulating toll-like receptors (TLRs) and through modulation of cytokines and chemokines.

Promastigotes resist complement attack. They can alter certain toll-like receptors (TLRs) on the cells of the immune system to reduce recognition of the parasite and inhibit killing by macrophages. Amastigotes survive in the phagosome by producing various virulence factors and altering host cell signaling. Leishmania also evade detection by T-lymphocytes and interfere with macrophage antigen presentation.

Amastigotes can either remain in the skin (CL), or disseminate to give rise to diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis (DCL) or to the mucosa (ML). Some species invade the reticuloendothelial system, liver, and spleen (often without any skin lesion) to cause visceral leishmaniasis (VL). The incubation period is usually 2 weeks to 3 months, but can be much longer.
See for the life cycle.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Living in or traveling to an endemic area and exposure to infected sand flies
Young age, immunosuppression, including HIV co-infection increases risk of dissemination / severe disease

list.listitem: Sand fly control, prevention of bites with indoor residual spraying, bed nets, screens, insect repellent, covering skin with clothing at night, and treated curtains and dog collars are important for disease prevention. B
There are no current recommendations for screening, primary prophylaxis, or preemptive treatment of asymptomatic individuals. C
Rapid identification, treatment, and monitoring systems are needed to prevent spread in endemic regions with the appropriate vectors present. C
There is no current recommendation for routine screening of asymptomatic individuals.

The leishmaniasis (or Montenegro) skin test is used in South America, but is neither available nor recommended, in the United States today. It cannot distinguish between active and resolved infections and is negative in active visceral leishmaniasis.
An iterferon-y release assay is currently being developed, but has not been validated for clinical use.

Prevention methods include controlling the vector population with insecticides, culling or treating animal reservoirs, and preventing humans from being infected through use of personal protective equipment and bed nets.
There are several licensed vaccines for dogs as they are a primary reservoir but currently there are no human vaccines.
Immunity to homologous species reinfection does occur in endemic regions after infection.
Treatment monitoring and proper reporting are lacking in many areas of the world.

Suspect leishmaniasis in patients exposed in endemic regions with either typical lesions for cutaneous or mucosal leishmaniasis, or with systemic signs such as fever, malaise, and abdominal pain for visceral leishmaniasis. C

There is no single best-test for diagnosis. Multiple tests should be performed to increase the diagnostic yield, including microscopy to look for tissue amastigotes, in vitro culture, DNA PCR, and in the case of visceral leishmaniasis, serologic testing. C
Contact the CDC (404-718-4745) or the Leishmania Diagnostic Laboratory at the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research (240-595-7353) for assistance in diagnosis and management. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Enlarging patch with red border and central clearing. More serious infections such as chromomycosis, maduromycosis, paracoccidioidomycosis, coccidioidomycosis, sporotrichosis, and histoplasmosis may cause chronic ulcers and other skin lesions.
Papules and vesicles that evolve into brown or yellow crusts, scarring depends on depth of infection. Frank pus or impetiginous appearance may be present.
Nodules which ulcerate with new lesions occurring along regional lymph pathways.
Single or multiple firm painless nodule(s) that ulcerates with an undermined edge.
Initial papule becomes a raised “papilloma” with secondary lesions, lymphadenopathy.
Painless chancre, usually on the genitals, heals without scarring.
Chronic ulcers, fistulae and abscesses, lupus vulgaris, other signs of tuberculosis.
Patches and nodules, hypopigmented lesions often without sensation, enlarged tender nerves.
Chronic ulcers with raised edges. Kaposi's sarcoma are red-violet nodules with a chronic course.
Small macules or papules from granulomas, lupus pernio, erythema nodosum.

Differential.Differential_Name: Mucosal leishmaniasis includes many of the above diagnoses plus the following three diseases

Differential.Differential_Features: Destruction of nasal and upper airway sites. Mostly NK/T cell lymphomas.
Ulcerative lesions in the nasopharynx.
Necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis in many sites including nasal septum and sinuses.

Differential.Differential_Name: Chronic malaria (tropical splenomegaly, hyperreactive malarial splenomegaly)
Differential.Differential_Features: Massive splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, anemia.
Cough, weight loss, fatigue, fever, hepatosplenomegaly, skin lesions.
Hepatosplenomegaly, portal hypertension, varices, ascites.
Weight loss, abdominal pain, abdominal mass, malabsorption, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly.
Fever, weight loss, sweats, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, pulmonary TB.
Fever, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, tachycardia, cardiomegaly, CNS lesions if immunocompromised.
Fever, chills, sweats, joint pains, tender splenomegaly.
Fever, headache, abdominal pain, hepatosplenomegaly.
Fever, heart murmur, tender splenomegaly.
Fever, tender hepatomegaly, diarrhea.
Weight loss, edema, muscle wasting, hair changes, hepatomegaly.

list.listitem: Are usually on areas of exposed skin and may be solitary or contain multiple satellite lesions. (see and ).
Are usually on areas of exposed skin and may be solitary or contain multiple satellite lesions.
Lesions begin as small pink or red papules and enlarges into a nodule or plaque-like sore.
Central ulceration is common and may have indurated margins. Lesions are often painless (see and ).
Rarer cutaneous forms include the following:

Diffuse cutaneous (DCL): diffuse nodular non-ulcerating lesions that occur over the body after an initial cutaneous lesion. It can persist for years and is usually associated with L. mexicana in the Americas and L. aethiopica in Africa. Likely due to defective cellular response to Leishmania antigens.
Leishmaniasis recidivans (LR): nodules and ulcerating lesions occurring at the border of a healed primary ulcer/scar. It can last for years and is usually associated with L. tropica infection.

Post Kala-Azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL): chronic skin lesions, patches, and nodules, occurring after treatment for VL caused by L. donovani. Lesions resemble Leprosy, but lack sensorineural changes. Parasite load is high and it is a reservoir of infection to others if in an endemic area.

Patients often have a history of CL with later development of lesions of the nasal mucosa, often involving the palate, with erythema, edema, nodules, and ulcers with erosion. Patients with confirmed cutaneous leishmaniasis acquired in Central or South America should be evaluated for mucosal involvement.
Characterized by mucosal destruction of the nose, mouth, or nasal septum, but may also involve other structures of the head and neck such as the palate, pharynx, larynx, and trachea.
Sub-acute to chronic constitutional symptoms of fever (classically descrided as twice daily), malaise, and weight loss. There is often painful splenomegaly and hepatomegaly
Advanced disease is associated with cachexia, hypoalbuminemia with edema, pancytopenia, and signs and symptoms of liver failure including jaundice and ascites
Disease may be more severe when seen in combination with HIV or immunosuppression.

Tissue specimens (full-thickness punch or shave biopsy, a press imprint smear, lesion scraping, slit smear, lesion aspirate) should be sent for histopathology, PCR, and parasite culture. Species identification should be done upfront if possible. Serology in CL lacks sensitivity / specificity.
The CL Detect Rapid Test for Leishmania antigens have been approved by the FDA, and if available, can use tissue brushings as a rapid point-of-care diagnostic test.

Tissue aspiration and biopsy, preferably from the bone marrow, is the recommended initial test. Specimens are sent for microscopy, histopathology, culture and PCR. Other biopsy sites include the liver, spleen (most dangerous due to risk of hemorhage despite higher sensitivity than bone marrow), lymph node, or the buffy coat of peripheral blood.

DNA-based assays are the most sensitive and can diagnose recurrence. Serologic tests can be useful in VL (in contrast to CL), testing for antibodies against Leishmania k39 antigen. Serology can support the diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis, but should not be used as a stand-alone diagnostic test. PCR testing of blood is not widely validated so should be used in combination with other diagnostic tools, and not as a stand-alone test.These tests cannot be used to assess response to therapy.
See the algorithms for a recommended approach to evaluation of the patient with suspected cutaneous or mucosal leishmaniasis in or visceral leishmaniasis in .

Recommend testing through reference laboratories: Center for Disease Control and Prevention in Atlanta, Georgia (404-718-4745), or the Leishmania Diagnostic Laboratory at the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research in Silver Spring, Maryland (240-595-7353) for US service members and their beneficiaries, and DOD civilian employees only.

Uncomplicated CL may not need to be treated, but if warranted, topical therapy options include cryotherapy, thermotherapy, photodynamic therapy, intralesional pentavalent antimony, and topical paromomycin. B

Cases of CL that are at risk of ML based on infecting species and/or geographic exposure (Latin America), will require a thorough ENT exam to assess for ML, which can significantly influence treatment. C
Complicated CL is treated with systemic therapy, either oral azoles and miltefosine, or parenteral pentavalent antimony, amphotericin B, or pentamidine. C

ML is treated with systemic therapy. Options include pentavalent antimonials, amphotericin B, and miltefosine. Depending on risk of airway compromise, treatment may require inpatient monitoring and corticosteroids. C
VL is treated with systemic therapy, preferably liposomal amphotericin-B (L-AmB), or pentavalent antimonials, paromomycin, and miltefosine. C
Treatment should be individualized. C
Therapies outlined in
Some CL infections seem to resolve spontaneously (observation for 4-6 wks is reasonable), although the parasite may persist indefinitely in the macrophage, held in check by cell-mediated immunity.
It is important to distinguish between uncomplicated CL and complicated CL as that directs therapy.
Uncomplicated CL is characterized by no mucosal involvement nor infection by species associated with mucosal disease, single and small lesions, in an immunocompetent host.

Complicated CL is characterized by mucosal involvement or infection with species associated with mucosal disease, large or multiple lesions, an immunosuppressed host, or clinical failure after prior treatment.
A randomized trial of 135 patients with CL randomized them to systemic versus intralesional meglumine antimoniate. Intralesional therapy was similarly effective and better tolerated.
Always treat immunosuppressed patients. Treat unless lesion(s) is minor, healing, and not potentially associated with mucosal disease.

For uncomplicated CL that does not spontaneously resolve, or in a patient who prefers to be treated, local therapy including cryotherapy, thermotherapy, photodynamic therapy, intralesional pentavalent antimony, or topical paromomycin can be considered.

For more extensive CL or ML use liposomal amphotericin-B (L-AmB) if available. Pentavalent antimony is the second choice, but no parenteral therapy is approved in the United States for CL. Miltefosine is approved for disease due to Viannia subspecies. ML is treated parentally first, sometimes with steroids for inflammation of the larynx.
Mucosal disease requires systemic therapy. Agents include parenteral pentavalent antimony, amphotericin B, and miltefosine.

Complete examination of the naso-oropharyngeal and laryngeal mucosa prior to initiation of therapy. If there is high risk of respiratory obstruction, inpatient monitoring during treatment and prophylactic corticosteroids are recommend to reduce risk of respiratory compromise. 100

VL requires systemic treatment. Liposomal amphotericin B is the only FDA approved drug; other options include amphotericin B deoxycholate, parenteral pentavalent antimonials, parenteral paromomycin, and miltefosine .

A randomized trial compared liposomal amphotericin B (single dose 7.g mg/kg) + 14 days of miltefosine (2.5 mg/kg/day) with miltefosine 2.5 mg/kg/day for 28 days in 144 patients. The clinical cure rate was 100% in both groups at the end of therapy, but at 6 months 17% in the miltefosine monotherapy group compared with none in the combination therapy group had a relapse of their disease.
Species-level identification can influence choice of first-line agent due to geography-associated efficacy data.

Post Kala-azar Dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) is treated with the same medications as VL but requires a more prolonged course (12-16 weeks). Miltefosine resistance has been reported in India and combination therapy is being studied for this disorder.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis should be treated parenterally. Visceral leishmaniasis diagnosis is more difficult and the presentation is often atypical. Leishmania identification by histopathology, PCR, and culture of a tissue biopsy is still the best approach.

Visceral leishmaniasis acts synergistically with HIV infection. Antiretroviral therapy should always be initiated concurrently, or before, leishmaniasis treatment. The relapse rate approaches 90% if patient is not on HAART (highly active antiretroviral therapy) in advance, and can occur long after initial antileishmanial treatment. Chronic intermittent suppressive therapy may be needed if the CD4 count is below 200 cells/mm3. Monitor for and treat relapses.

Liposomal amphotericin-B (L-AmB) therapy is recommended in the United States, but may require higher doses for extended time. L-AmB is approved in the United States at a dose of 4 mg/Kg/day IV on days 1-5, 10, 17, 24, 31, 38 for total of 40 mg/Kg. Some limited data suggests using combination therapy, L-AmB plus miltefosine (optimal duration not yet defined).

In East Africa, higher doses of L-AmB may be needed and the treatment of choice is pentavalent antimonials combined with paromomycin. (However, IV paromomycin is not available in the United States). The pentavalent antimonial drugs tend to be poorly tolerated in patients with HIV co-infection and there is no data for paromomycin.
Wound care should be performed for CL to prevent bacterial superinfection.
Cosmetic surgery or skin grafts for CL, and surgical reconstruction for ML, may be necessary and should be delayed for at least one year after healing.
Supportive therapy to optimize nutritional status and treatment of secondary infections also play important roles in treatment outcomes.
CL is not fatal unless it progresses to ML or disseminated to VL, but scars can be disfiguring and have negative psychosocial impacte. B
VL is over 90% fatal if not treated and has a 4% case fatality rate even with treatment. B
There is a long post-treatment follow-up given risk of relapse. HIV and leishmaniasis co-infected individuals should be monitored indefinitely until effective immune reconstitution.B

Cutaneous leishmaniasis: The incubation period can be as short as a week or as long as 3 years depending on the species. Spontaneous cure rates vary by species and geography, but eventually nearly everyone will heal unless there is dissemination, immunocompromise, or other complication. Lesions can persist for months or years with parasites found in healed scars even after antimonial treatment.

Mucocsal leishmaniasis: Mucosal lesions usually occur within several years after the cutaneous infection. ML can be destructive and disfiguring, and rarely, can cause respiratory compromise and death.

Visceral leishmaniasis: If untreated, >90% fatal, either directly or from complications (hemorrhage, secondary infection). Even with treatment, the case-fatality rate is 4%. Older individuals, plus those with malnutrition, edema, tuberculosis, or HIV infection, have higher mortality rates.
CL will heal with scarring but relapses can occur. Parasites generally remain even if the skin lesions heal.
VL has about a 4% mortality rate even if treated. Relapses can occur.
Post Kala-Azar dermal leishmaniasis occurs after treatment for VL and serves as a reservoir to infect others.
Treated leishmaniasis cases should be monitored for at least 12 months. Cases at risk for ML get 2 yr monitoring.
Most relapses of VL occur within 6-18 months.
HIV co-infection patients are monitored until effective immune reconstitution.

Both VL and ML should be treated in pregnancy. VL is associated with abortion, preterm deliveries, small infants, maternal death, and congenital infection. L-AmB is recommended over pentavalent antimony. Miltefosine is contraindicated in pregnancy and lactation.
Treatment for CL is usually deferred until after pregnancy if possible.

td.strong: Local Therapy for Uncomplicated CL lesions

tr.td: Cryotherapy
Efficacy 53%-100%, better if combined with intralesional antimonials. Various regimens, i.e. freeze 15-20 seconds thaw and refreeze. May repeat in 3 weeks for up to 3 sessions
Thermotherapy
Cure rates of 54%-73% using a radiofrequency unit. Apply for 1-3 thirty-second sessions
Intralesional pentavalent antimony

Usually for small lesions, often in combination with cryotherapy. Intralesional antimonials not approved for use in the U.S. Various regimens, i.e. 0.2-0.5 ml per session every 3-7 days or up to 3 weeks
Paromomycin cream (15%)
This is a topical aminoglycoside and is often used for small ulcerating lesions caused by L.L. major. Applied BID for 10 days, rest for 10 days, and applied BID for 10 more days.
Photodynamic Therapy

A newer form of therapy that uses light to sensitize an administered photosensitizer to create reactive oxygen species which then destroys cells and tissues. This is currently being studied, but early reports show >90% success rate with minimal cosmetic effects. (REF - Asilian, A. & Davami, M. Comparison between the efficacy of photodynamic therapy and topical paromomycin in the treatment of Old World cutaneous leishmaniasis: a placebo-controlled, randomized clinical trial. Clin. Exp. Dermatol. 31, 634–637 (2006).

td.strong: Oral Systemic Therapy for Complicated CL

tr.td: Azoles

Efficacy of different azoles is dependent on infecting species, so species-level identification is important. Regimens include fluconazole PO 200 mg daily for 6 weeks and ketoconazole PO 600 mg daily for 28 days. (REF - Aronson, N. et al. Diagnosis and treatment of leishmaniasis: clinical practice guidelines by the infectious diseases society of america (IDSA) and the american society of tropical medicine and hygiene (ASTMH). Clin. Infect. Dis. 63, e202–e264 (2016).)
Miltefosine (also used for ML and VL)

Efficacy varies by species and geography. It is the only drug approved by the FDA specifically for CL due to Viannia subspecies. Dosing for CL and ML is the same: 50mg PO BID if 30-44 kg, give 50 mg TID for 28 days if ≥45 kg . Contraindicated in pregnant / breastfeeding women.

td.strong: Parenteral Systemic Therapy for Complicated CL and ML

tr.td: Pentavalent antimonials (sodium stibogluconate [Pentostam] or meglumine antimoniate[Glucantime])

Useful to prevent progression to mucosal disease and for more complicated lesions. Both drugs considered clinically equivalent with efficacy ranges up to 91% in some trials. Available from the CDC on IND protocol. Side effects include QT prolongation, pancreatitis, myalgia, vomiting, abdominal pain, fever, and rash. CL dose is 20 mg of Sb/kg/day for 20 days. ML dose is 20 mg of Sb/kg/day for 28 days. (REF- Aronson, N. et al. Diagnosis and treatment of leishmaniasis: clinical practice guidelines by the infectious diseases society of america (IDSA) and the american society of tropical medicine and hygiene (ASTMH). Clin. Infect. Dis. 63, e202–e264 (2016). A randomized trial of 135 patients with CL randomized them to systemic versus intralesional Meglumine Antimoniate. Intralesional therapy was similarly effective and better tolerated.
Amphotericin B deoxycholate

Use is limited by long infusion times and multiple adverse effects including hypokalemia, phlebitis, fevers and rigors, and irreversible nephrotoxicity. Dose for CL is 0.5-1.0 mg/kg daily or every other day for a total cumulative dose of 15-30 mg/kg, or for a total cumulative dose of 20-45 mg/kg for ML. (REF - Aronson, N. et al. Diagnosis and treatment of leishmaniasis: clinical practice guidelines by the infectious diseases society of america (IDSA) and the american society of tropical medicine and hygiene (ASTMH). Clin. Infect. Dis. 63, e202–e264 (2016)
Liposomal amphotericin B (L-AmB)

Efficacy 80%-85% in some studies. While better tolerated with lower rates of nephrotoxicity compared to deoxycholate formulation, the same side effect profile can still be seen. Unclear optimal dosing regimen. One CL dosing regimen is 3 mg/kg on days 1-5 and a sixth dose on day 10, or dosed on days 1-7; total of 18-21 mg/kg5. For ML dosing is 3 mg/kg/day for a total of 20-60 mg/kg.
Pentamidine

Second line due to side effects(electrolye abnormalities, hypoglycemia, pancreatitis). Efficacy is similar to pentavalent antimonials, 73%-95% and use limited mainly to L.V. guyanensis. CL dosing 3 mg/kg every other day for 3-4 doses. ML dosing is 2-4mg/kg every other day or TIW for 15 or more doses .
Liposomal amphotericin B (L-AmB)

The only FDA approved drug for treatment of VL in the United States, and the drug of choice in pregnancy (REF - Meyerhoff, A. U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval of AmBisome (liposomal amphotericin B) for treatment of visceral leishmaniasis. Clin. Infect. Dis. 28, 42–8; discussion 49 (1999). There are different dosing schedules used around the world. FDA-approved regimen for immunocompetent individuals is 3 mg/kg on days 1-5, 14, and 21 for a total of 21 mg/kg; FDA-approved regimen for immunosuppressed individuals is 4 mg/kg on days 1-5, 10, 17, 24, 31, and 38 for a total dose of 40 mg/kg.
Amphotericin B deoxycholate

Numerous adverse side effects as elaborated above. Off-label dosing is 1 mg/kg daily or every other day for a total of 15-20 doses. (REF- Aronson, N. et al. Diagnosis and treatment of leishmaniasis: clinical practice guidelines by the infectious diseases society of america (IDSA) and the american society of tropical medicine and hygiene (ASTMH). Clin. Infect. Dis. 63, e202–e264 (2016).
Pentavalent Antimony (sodium stibogluconate (pentostam) or meglumine antimoniate (Glucantime))
(see above) 20 mg Sb/kg/day for 28 days
Miltefosine
The only oral agent approved for VL, must be adults over 30 kg. Contraindicated in pregnancy and breast feeding. Dosing is the same as above for CL and ML.
Paromomycin

IV and IM formulations are currently under investigation in multiple countries. Reported efficacy as high as 77-97%. (REF-Jha, T. K. et al. Randomised controlled trial of aminosidine (paromomycin) v sodium stibogluconate for treating visceral leishmaniasis in North Bihar, India. BMJ 316, 1200–1205 (1998) Used in India as IV or IM at 15 mg/kg/day for 21 days. (REF - Sundar, S., Jha, T. K., Thakur, C. P., Sinha, P. K. & Bhattacharya, S. K. Injectable paromomycin for Visceral leishmaniasis in India. N. Engl. J. Med. 356, 2571–2581 (2007).
Pentamidine isethionate
Second-line therapy due to adverse drug effects. Dosing is 4 mg/kg every other day or TIW for a total of 15-30 doses.
Combination regimens are being used to allow shorter courses and to reduce resistance
L-AmB is combined with miltefosine in India or sodium stibogluconate is combined with paromomycin in Africa, for example
